title: Aon's Third-Quarter Organic Revenue Grows 6% and Adjusted EPS Rises 10% to $3.36, With the USI Acquisition Expected to Close in the Fourth Quarter
summary: Aon reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $4,101 million, up 3%, with 6% organic growth, GAAP diluted EPS of $2.23, adjusted EPS of $3.36 versus $3.05, a wider adjusted operating margin of 27.0% and no share repurchases in the quarter, while it expects its USI acquisition to close in the fourth quarter.
description:
Aon, the professional services and insurance brokerage group, has published its results for the third quarter of 2026. The figures below come from the company's results release as carried by the financial data site Finviz. The Securities and Exchange Commission filing itself could not be retrieved, so the numbers are those reproduced in the release text. Aon reports several non-GAAP measures that it defines itself, and this article keeps them separate from the GAAP figures wherever the release does. Percentage changes marked as arithmetic are calculated here, not quoted.

The headline numbers

Total revenue for the quarter was $4,101 million, compared with $3,997 million a year earlier, an increase of 3%. Organic revenue growth, which removes the effect of currency, acquisitions and divestitures and certain fiduciary investment income, was 6%. By solution line it was 7% in Commercial Risk Solutions, 7% in Reinsurance Solutions, 6% in Health Solutions and 4% in Wealth Solutions. The gap between 3% reported growth and 6% organic growth shows that non-organic items, such as currency and the sale of businesses, reduced reported revenue growth. The release does not break the difference down in the portion reviewed.

GAAP net income attributable to Aon shareholders was $476 million, up from $458 million, or 4%. Diluted earnings per share under GAAP were $2.23, against $2.11, up 6%. Adjusted net income attributable to shareholders was $715 million against $660 million, up 8%, and adjusted diluted earnings per share were $3.36 against $3.05, up 10%. The adjusted figures are higher than the GAAP figures because Aon excludes items such as amortization and impairment of intangible assets, expenses of its Accelerating Aon United Program, changes in contingent consideration, integration costs related to the NFP acquisition and transaction costs for USI.

Margins

Operating income was $809 million against $816 million, a fall of 1%, and the GAAP operating margin was 19.7% against 20.4%, a decline of 70 basis points. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point. On an adjusted basis, operating income was $1,106 million against $1,051 million, up 5%, and the adjusted operating margin was 27.0% against 26.3%, up 70 basis points. The two margins moved in opposite directions, which means that the costs Aon excludes from its adjusted measure grew in the quarter. Readers should therefore treat the improved adjusted margin as management's preferred view and the GAAP margin as the unadjusted one.

Cash and capital

Operating cash flow was $1,191 million against $1,148 million. The release defines free cash flow as cash flow from operating activities less capital expenditures, and reports $1,097 million against $1,079 million, up 2%. Aon repurchased no shares in the third quarter, and about $7.7 billion of its repurchase authorization remained available at September 30, 2026. The absence of buybacks is consistent with the company's stated priority, described below, of repaying debt after the USI deal.

Nine months

For the first nine months of 2026, revenue was $13,381 million against $12,881 million, up 4%, with organic growth of 5%. Operating income was $3,439 million against $3,136 million, up 10%, and the operating margin was 25.7% against 24.3%. Adjusted operating income was $4,299 million against $4,038 million, up 6%, with an adjusted margin of 32.1% against 31.3%. Diluted EPS was $10.46 against $9.21, up 14%, and adjusted diluted EPS was $13.66 against $12.22, up 12%. Free cash flow for the period was $1,943 million against $1,895 million, up 3%. Over the nine months, then, the GAAP margin improved, unlike in the third quarter alone.

The USI acquisition and outlook

The release says the acquisition of USI is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. Management's priority afterwards is to repay debt, with a path to bring leverage down to its 2.8x to 3.0x objective in about 24 months. The release defines leverage as total debt divided by trailing 12-month EBITDA. It gives no numeric guidance for revenue or earnings per share. On currency, it says that if exchange rates hold, there would be a de minimis effect on fourth-quarter adjusted EPS and a favorable effect of about $0.42 per share on full-year 2026 adjusted EPS. Chief executive Greg Case is quoted as saying that the impact of the company's strategy is further demonstrated by its strong third-quarter results, and management says it enters the fourth quarter with significant momentum, which it believes reinforces confidence in its full-year performance. These are the company's own characterizations.

A comparison with other brokers

Organic growth of 6% sits above the 4% to 5% reported by Gallagher and well above the 1.2% reported by Brown & Brown for the same quarter, according to those companies' releases. Comparisons between brokers should be made with care, because each defines organic growth slightly differently and the businesses differ in mix: Aon has large reinsurance, health and wealth operations, while the others are weighted to retail and wholesale brokerage.

What to watch

Three points follow. First, the closing of USI and the pace of debt reduction, since buybacks were paused in the quarter. Second, whether organic growth holds at the current level as commercial insurance prices fall, because lower premiums reduce commission bases. Third, the gap between GAAP and adjusted margins, which depends on integration and restructuring spending that the release excludes from its adjusted figures.

Limits

This article summarizes a company results release as reproduced by a data site. The last part of that page was not read, so some footnotes may be missing. It is general information, not investment advice.
source_name: Aon plc (third-quarter 2026 results release, via Finviz)
image_alt: Office towers representing a global insurance broker (illustrative)
key_points: Total revenue was $4,101 million against $3,997 million, up 3%, and organic revenue growth was 6%: Commercial Risk Solutions 7%, Reinsurance Solutions 7%, Health Solutions 6% and Wealth Solutions 4%.
GAAP net income attributable to Aon shareholders was $476 million ($2.23 diluted EPS) against $458 million ($2.11), while adjusted diluted EPS rose 10% to $3.36 from $3.05.
Operating margin fell to 19.7% from 20.4%, but adjusted operating margin widened to 27.0% from 26.3%.
Free cash flow was $1,097 million against $1,079 million, Aon made no share repurchases in the quarter, and about $7.7 billion of authorization remained at September 30.

Management expects the USI acquisition to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, with debt repayment the priority and a path back to a 2.8x to 3.0x leverage objective in about 24 months; the release gives no numeric revenue or EPS guidance.
why_it_matters: Aon is one of the world's largest insurance and reinsurance brokers, so its results show how demand for risk advice, reinsurance placements and health and wealth consulting is holding up while insurance prices fall. The gap between GAAP and adjusted figures also shows how much acquisition and restructuring cost is in the numbers.

title: Brown & Brown's Third-Quarter Organic Revenue Grows Just 1.2% as Revenue Rises 7.4% to $1.73 Billion, While Diluted EPS Slips to $0.67 and the Adjusted EBITDAC Margin Falls Two Points
summary: Brown & Brown reported third-quarter 2026 revenues of $1,725 million, up 7.4%, but organic revenue grew only 1.2%, diluted EPS fell to $0.67 from $0.68, adjusted EPS rose to $1.07 and the adjusted EBITDAC margin declined to 34.6% from 36.6%.
description:
Brown & Brown, one of the largest independent insurance brokers in the United States, has reported its results for the third quarter and the first nine months of 2026. The figures below come from the company's results release, filed as Exhibit 99.1 to a Form 8-K. The release states that final third-quarter results may differ from these preliminary, unaudited figures. It gives consolidated numbers only: segment-level organic growth for retail, programs, wholesale brokerage and services is not in it, and neither is any forward guidance. Where this article calculates a figure, it says so.

Revenue: strong headline, weak underlying growth

Total revenues for the quarter were $1,725 million, compared with $1,606 million a year earlier, an increase of $119 million, or 7.4%. Commissions and fees, the largest part of revenue, were $1,700 million against $1,550 million, up 9.7%. Those headline numbers include revenue from acquired businesses. The company's organic revenue measure, which excludes contingent commissions, operations acquired in the last 12 months, divested business, foreign currency translation and litigation-related effects, was $1,464 million against $1,447 million. That is an increase of $17 million, or 1.2%. Including contingent commissions, which are bonuses paid by insurers depending on volume or results, organic revenue was $1,543 million against $1,520 million, up $23 million, or 1.5%. The company reports that acquisitions added $156 million of commissions and fees in the quarter, which are excluded from the organic figure.

The gap between 9.7% growth in commissions and fees and 1.2% organic growth is the main point of the quarter. Most of the reported increase came from businesses bought rather than from selling more to existing clients. The release's description of the chief executive's comment is that the third quarter reflected the efforts of teammates to win more customers, and that about 5,000 teammates joined from Accession just over a year ago.

Profit and margins

Income before income taxes was $320 million against $311 million, up 2.9%, and the pre-tax margin was 18.6% against 19.4%, a decline of 0.8 percentage points. Net income attributable to the company was $240 million against $227 million, up 5.7%. Diluted earnings per share were $0.67 against $0.68, a decrease of 1.5%, which is lower even though net income rose, because the number of shares was larger after the 2025 offering. The release does not itemize the share count in the portion reviewed, so that explanation is an inference from the figures. Adjusted diluted EPS, which excludes items such as earn-out changes, disposal gains or losses, acquisition and integration costs and amortization, was $1.07 against $1.05, up 1.9%.

EBITDAC means earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and changes in estimated acquisition earn-out payables. It was $575 million against $529 million, with a margin of 33.3% against 32.9%. Adjusted EBITDAC, which also excludes disposal gains or losses, acquisition and integration costs and an escrow mark-to-market item, was $597 million against $587 million, up 1.7%, and its margin fell to 34.6% from 36.6%, a decline of 2.0 points. The two margins therefore moved in opposite directions. The release does not explain why the two diverged; the difference lies in the size of the items each measure excludes. The release also notes that the 2025 quarter includes about $29 million of interest income from offering and notes proceeds that were held for the Accession purchase, which inflates the prior-year base against which this year's profit is compared.

Nine months

For the first nine months, total revenues were $5,302 million against $4,295 million, up 23.4%, and commissions and fees were $5,234 million against $4,183 million. Organic revenue was $3,987 million against $3,977 million, up only 0.3%, and with contingents it was $4,200 million against $4,138 million, up 1.5%. Acquisitions contributed $985 million of the revenue. Net income attributable to the company was $954 million against $790 million, up 20.8%, yet diluted EPS was flat at $2.57, and adjusted diluted EPS rose 5.7% to $3.52 from $3.33. Adjusted EBITDAC was $1,927 million against $1,594 million, up 20.9%, with an adjusted margin of 36.3% against 37.1%.

Cash flow and the balance sheet

Operating cash flow for the nine months was $1,140 million against $1,006 million. Cash spent on acquisitions was $41 million, compared with $7,659 million in the same period of 2025, which reflects the absence of a deal on the scale of Accession this year. The company bought back $750 million of its own stock. At September 30, 2026, total assets were $29,448 million and total equity was $12,601 million.

How to read it

Three points stand out. Organic growth near 1% means that, apart from acquisitions, revenue is barely growing, which is consistent with a softening insurance market in which lower premiums reduce commissions. The margin decline suggests costs are rising faster than underlying revenue. And the year-over-year profit growth leans on acquired earnings and a comparison period that includes unusual interest income. The release provides no outlook, so there is no company statement about whether organic growth will improve.

Limits

This article summarizes a company release containing unaudited figures and does not include analyst estimates or the share-price reaction. The explanation of the EPS decline is an inference. It is general information, not investment advice.
source_name: Brown & Brown, Inc. (third-quarter 2026 results, Exhibit 99.1 to Form 8-K)
image_alt: Financial statements and a calculator representing quarterly results (illustrative)
key_points: Total revenues were $1,725 million against $1,606 million, up 7.4%, with commissions and fees of $1,700 million, but organic revenue was $1,464 million against $1,447 million, growth of only 1.2%.
Net income attributable to the company was $240 million against $227 million, yet diluted EPS slipped to $0.67 from $0.68, while adjusted diluted EPS rose 1.9% to $1.07.
Adjusted EBITDAC was $597 million against $587 million, but the adjusted margin fell to 34.6% from 36.6%, and the unadjusted EBITDAC margin rose to 33.3% from 32.9%.
Acquisitions contributed $156 million of commissions and fees in the quarter and $985 million over nine months, when total revenues rose 23.4% to $5,302 million while organic revenue grew 0.3%.
The release gives no segment-level organic growth and no forward guidance; the prior-year comparison includes about $29 million of interest income on funds held for the Accession acquisition.
why_it_matters: Brown & Brown is a large US insurance broker that bought Accession in 2025, so its reported growth is dominated by acquisitions. Organic growth of about 1% shows how little underlying growth is left when insurance prices fall, which is the figure that matters for judging the business apart from deals.

title: GIC Re's Second-Quarter Standalone Profit After Tax Is Rs 2,456 Crore on Gross Premiums of Rs 11,228 Crore, With an Underwriting Loss Offset by Investment Income
summary: General Insurance Corporation of India reported standalone second-quarter FY27 profit after tax of Rs 2,45,562 lakh (about Rs 2,456 crore) on gross premiums written of Rs 11,22,821 lakh, with an underwriting loss of about Rs 1,080 crore more than covered by Rs 2,815 crore of investment income, and half-year profit of about Rs 4,378 crore.
description:
General Insurance Corporation of India, known as GIC Re, is India's national reinsurer. It has reported unaudited standalone results for the quarter and half year ended September 30, 2026, the second quarter of the 2026-27 financial year (Q2 FY27). The figures in this article come from a single secondary report by InvestyWise, which says it is based on a filing with the exchanges. The filing itself was not reviewed. The report gives its figures in lakh rupees; one lakh is 100,000 and one crore is 10 million, so crore amounts below are conversions made for this article. The report does not give prior-year figures, consolidated results, a combined ratio or a solvency ratio, so none appear here.

The quarter

For the quarter ended September 30, 2026, GIC Re reported gross premiums written of Rs 11,22,821 lakh, about Rs 11,228 crore. Net premiums written, which are premiums retained after the reinsurer's own reinsurance purchases, were Rs 10,56,203 lakh, about Rs 10,562 crore, and net premiums earned were Rs 10,55,968 lakh, about Rs 10,560 crore. Total income was Rs 13,46,945 lakh, about Rs 13,469 crore, and total expenses were Rs 11,63,933 lakh, about Rs 11,639 crore. Subtracting expenses from income, an exercise done here, leaves about Rs 1,830 crore, which matches the operating profit of Rs 1,83,012 lakh reported.

Profit after tax was Rs 2,45,562 lakh, about Rs 2,456 crore. That is larger than the reported operating profit of about Rs 1,830 crore. The report does not explain the bridge between the two, so readers should not assume a particular cause. Items below operating profit, such as other income or tax effects, would be where the difference arises, but the report does not itemize them.

An underwriting loss, offset by investments

The most informative numbers are the underwriting loss and the investment income. The report gives an underwriting loss of Rs 1,07,965 lakh, about Rs 1,080 crore, for the quarter. An underwriting loss means that claims and operating costs on the reinsurance business exceeded the premiums earned. Net income from investments was Rs 2,81,531 lakh, about Rs 2,815 crore. A simple sum, calculated here, shows that investment income was about 2.6 times the size of the underwriting loss (2,815 divided by 1,080). In other words, the quarter's profit rested on the return from the reinsurer's investment portfolio and not on its reinsurance results. The report does not say what portion of the investment income was recurring interest and dividends and what portion came from selling assets, which matters for judging whether it can be repeated.

The half year

For the six months ended September 30, 2026, gross premiums written were Rs 24,70,357 lakh, about Rs 24,704 crore, and net premiums written were Rs 23,22,615 lakh, about Rs 23,226 crore. Net premiums earned were Rs 21,64,114 lakh, about Rs 21,641 crore. Net income from investments was Rs 4,98,679 lakh, about Rs 4,987 crore, total income was Rs 26,79,983 lakh, about Rs 26,800 crore, and total expenses were Rs 23,52,210 lakh, about Rs 23,522 crore. The underwriting loss for the half year was Rs 1,88,097 lakh, about Rs 1,881 crore, operating profit was Rs 3,27,772 lakh, about Rs 3,278 crore, and profit after tax was Rs 4,37,766 lakh, about Rs 4,378 crore.

Comparing the half-year and quarterly figures, done here, the first quarter of the year had a smaller underwriting loss than the second: about Rs 801 crore against about Rs 1,080 crore, calculated as the half-year loss minus the second-quarter loss. Gross premiums written in the first quarter were therefore about Rs 13,475 crore, higher than the second quarter's Rs 11,228 crore. These are derived numbers, and the report does not comment on them.

Corporate disclosures

The board approved the results on October 30, 2026, according to the report. It also notes that Executive Director Jayashri Balkrishna has opted for voluntary retirement under the company's scheme and will leave her post as a key managerial personnel on being relieved from service. Related party transaction disclosures for the half year will be filed separately in XBRL format, a standard electronic reporting format.

What the report leaves out

The report describes robust growth in gross premiums written and an increase in operating profit, but without figures for either. It gives no prior-year numbers, so it is not possible to say how much premiums or profit changed. It gives no consolidated profit, which includes subsidiaries, and no solvency ratio, which measures capital against the regulatory requirement. It does not discuss claims, catastrophe losses or the effect of India's obligatory cessions, in which direct insurers are required to place part of their business with the national reinsurer. For those details readers need GIC Re's own filing and investor presentation.

Why it matters

A reinsurer that earns its profit from investments is exposed to financial markets, and its underwriting results are a separate measure of how well it prices risk. Both numbers need to be read together. For India's insurance market, GIC Re's premium volume of more than Rs 11,000 crore in a single quarter shows the scale of risk passing through the national reinsurer, though the report does not say how that compares with the past.

Limits

This article relies on one secondary report of unaudited standalone results and includes arithmetic by the author. Currency conversions are rounded. It is general information, not investment advice.
source_name: InvestyWise, reporting GIC Re's standalone results filed with the exchanges
image_alt: City skyline representing a national reinsurer (illustrative)
key_points: For the quarter ended September 30, 2026, GIC Re reported standalone profit after tax of Rs 2,45,562 lakh (about Rs 2,456 crore), on gross premiums written of Rs 11,22,821 lakh (about Rs 11,228 crore) and total income of Rs 13,46,945 lakh (about Rs 13,469 crore).
The reinsurer had an underwriting loss of Rs 1,07,965 lakh (about Rs 1,080 crore) and net income from investments of Rs 2,81,531 lakh (about Rs 2,815 crore), so investment income carried the profit.

For the half year, gross premiums written were Rs 24,70,357 lakh (about Rs 24,704 crore), the underwriting loss was Rs 1,88,097 lakh (about Rs 1,881 crore) and profit after tax was Rs 4,37,766 lakh (about Rs 4,378 crore).

why_it_matters: GIC Re is India's national reinsurer, so its results show what Indian insurers are ceding and how claims are developing. This quarter's profit came from investments, not underwriting, which is a pattern worth understanding when reading any insurer's results.

title: IAG Settles the Last Greensill Proceeding, the White Oak Claim of About A$170 Million, After Earlier Settlements of A$4 Billion and A$2.8 Billion, With Terms Confidential
summary: Insurance Australia Group told the ASX on October 28, 2026 that its subsidiary had agreed to resolve the White Oak claim of about A$170 million, the last of the Greensill proceedings, on confidential terms and without a material effect on its financial position or FY27 results, following earlier settlements of about A$4 billion and A$2.8 billion in face value.
description:
Insurance Australia Group, IAG, has settled the last of the court cases arising from the collapse of Greensill, the supply-chain finance company. Insurance Business Australia reported on October 28, 2026 that IAG told the Australian Securities Exchange that its subsidiary, Insurance Australia Limited (IAL), had agreed to resolve the White Oak claim. The details in this article come from that report. The settlement documents and court files were not reviewed, and the terms of the settlement are confidential.

The final case

The proceeding is White Oak Commercial Finance Europe (Non-Levered) Limited v Insurance Australia Limited, case number NSD 1039 of 2021 in the Federal Court of Australia. The claimant is White Oak. The respondents were IAL, BCC Trade Credit and BCC's former head of trade credit, Greg Brereton. Tokio Marine entities and the broker Marsh were drawn in through related claims and cross-claims. The case was one of eleven proceedings that the court managed together. White Oak claimed about A$170 million plus interest, measured by the aggregate face value of the policies it relied on.

What the dispute was about

The claims concerned trade credit insurance policies that were allegedly issued by BCC Trade Credit on behalf of IAL to Greensill entities. Trade credit insurance pays a seller or lender if a buyer fails to pay an invoice, and Greensill's financing relied on such cover for the receivables it bought. When Greensill collapsed in 2021, those who had financed it sought to claim. According to the report, a June 2026 Federal Court ruling recorded IAL's position that the policies were not valid and that BCC was not authorised to issue them. The report stresses that no court has ruled on whether BCC had authority to bind IAL. After about five years of litigation there is therefore no published reasoning on that question, which means the settlements leave open how far an insurer is bound by policies issued in its name by an agent.

Timeline of the final stretch

On September 24, 2026, lawyers said White Oak's claims were set for trial the following month. On October 6, 2026, the Federal Court ordered White Oak to provide A$5 million in security for costs, after IAL and the BCC and Tokio Marine parties argued that the vehicle was effectively in run-off with minimal assets. Security for costs is money a claimant must lodge to cover the other side's legal costs if the claimant loses. Earlier court rulings included an April order requiring disclosure of settlement documents and a June order to produce WhatsApp messages. The settlement was announced on October 28, within the month in which the report says the trial had been expected to start.

The earlier settlements

The White Oak resolution follows two much larger ones. In May 2026, IAL settled with Greensill Bank AG and its administrator, a claim of about A$4 billion in face value plus interest. In September 2026, it settled with Credit Suisse entities, a claim of about A$2.8 billion in face value plus interest. IAG said the Credit Suisse settlement would not materially affect its financial position or FY27 results, based on anticipated recoveries, including insurance, reinsurance and indemnities. Adding the three face values, a calculation made here, gives about A$6.97 billion of claimed policy value across the three settled matters, although face value is not the amount paid and the settlement sums are not disclosed.

IAG's statement on the financial effect

IAG said the Greensill settlements would not have a material impact on its financial position or on its FY27 financial results. The report notes that the release was authorised by chief executive Nick Hawkins and described the financial effect as consistent with IAG's previous disclosures. The report does not separately quantify the effect of the White Oak settlement, and since the terms are confidential, no payment figure is available.

Marsh and the costs

The report notes that the Financial Times had reported that Marsh covered the largest portion of the Credit Suisse settlement. It says that no party has confirmed this or how costs were split. It also points to Marsh's SEC filing, which shows a charge of US$144 million for the quarter to September 30 and US$569 million for nine months, net of insurance proceeds, tied to the Australian proceedings, and says the liability reflects the Greensill Bank and Credit Suisse settlements and related costs. These are reported figures from a filing the report cites, and this article has not checked the filing. They show that the costs of the litigation were spread beyond IAG, but they do not establish who bore which part of any settlement.

What the outcome means

For the insurance industry, the end of the cases removes a large contingent liability for IAG and closes a high-profile dispute over trade credit cover. It does not answer the legal question at the centre of the case, and so it offers no precedent on when a managing agent's policies bind an insurer. Brokers and insurers that use delegated authority arrangements, in which an agent issues policies on the insurer's behalf, may still read the dispute as a reason to check the scope of authority and the validity of policies they rely on, but the report draws no such rule from a court.

Limits

This article relies on a single trade-press report. Settlement terms are confidential, allegations in the proceedings were not tested by a court, and the Marsh figures come from a report of a filing that was not reviewed. It is general information, not legal advice.

title: NSW Indexes CTP Benefits From October 1, 2026, Lifting the Weekly Statutory Benefit Cap to A$3,853 and the Non-Economic Loss Cap to A$521,000, With Green Slip Effects Not Yet Quantified
summary: SIRA confirmed that New South Wales compulsory third party benefits were indexed from October 1, 2026, taking the maximum weekly statutory benefit to A$3,853 and the maximum non-economic loss damages to A$521,000, while the average Green Slip was A$536 in the year to June 2025 and the effect of the new indexation on premiums has not been quantified.
description:
The State Insurance Regulatory Authority of New South Wales, SIRA, has confirmed that a range of compulsory third party (CTP) scheme benefits were increased from October 1, 2026. Insurance Business Australia reported the change and suggested it would push Green Slip premiums higher. The details in this article come from that report. The orders themselves were not reviewed, and the report does not state the percentage by which benefits rose. Where this article makes a calculation or points out an inference, it says so.

What was indexed

CTP insurance, known in New South Wales as the Green Slip, pays benefits to people injured in motor accidents. The report says SIRA indexed several items under the Motor Accident Injuries Act 2017: legal costs, medico-legal fees, weekly benefit payments and non-economic damages. Damages under two older laws, the Motor Accidents Act 1988 and the Motor Accidents Compensation Act 1999, are also indexed, because claims under those laws are still open. Indexation is an automatic adjustment so that fixed dollar limits keep pace with wages. The report says the adjustment equals the percentage change in NSW average weekly total earnings as published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics. It cites the relevant sections of the 2017 Act, 3.22 for statutory benefits and 4.22 for the non-economic loss cap. SIRA published three orders: the Motor Accident Injuries (Indexation) Order (No. 2) 2026, the Motor Accidents (Determination of Non-Economic Loss) Order 2026 and the Motor Accidents Compensation (Determination of Loss) Order 2026.

The new caps

The report gives two headline figures. The maximum weekly statutory benefit, under section 3.9 of the 2017 Act, is A$3,853. The maximum non-economic loss damages, under section 4.13, is A$521,000. Non-economic loss damages compensate for things like pain, suffering and loss of enjoyment of life, as distinct from lost income or medical costs. The report does not state the previous figures, so the size of the increase cannot be calculated from it.

What happens to premiums

The report's headline says the indexation will push Green Slip premiums higher, but it does not give a figure. Its reasoning is that higher fee caps and payment thresholds feed into insurers' claims reserves, which influence pricing at renewal. Because the report does not quantify the effect, readers should treat the direction as plausible but unmeasured.

The latest premium data in the report comes from SIRA's CTP scheme performance report for the year to June 30, 2025. In that year the average Green Slip rose A$35, or 7%, to A$536 including levies and GST. That is still below the average of A$935 before the 2017 reforms. A comparison made here shows the average is about 43% lower than the pre-reform level (536 against 935), though the two figures are separated by years of inflation. Fund levies, which are included in the premium, also rose. The total average levies went from A$164.80 to A$190.60 between January 2025 and January 2026, and one component, the Motor Accidents Operational Fund levy, rose from A$37.50 to A$65.50.

The downward pressure that is easing

SIRA operates a transitional mechanism that recovers excess profits from CTP insurers. The report says it has recovered A$542.9 million since 2020 and that SIRA said it has led to a reduction in premiums. In September 2025, SIRA confirmed that no insurer profits would be reclaimed that year, reflecting insurers' pricing adjustments during the transition. The report says this downward pressure on prices is easing. Put together, the report describes premiums as rising from a lower base, with less clawback of profit and higher benefit caps.

What injured people can claim

The report summarizes how long statutory benefits last under the 2017 scheme. Most injured people can claim for up to 52 weeks regardless of fault. Threshold injuries are capped at 52 weeks of weekly payments. For non-threshold injuries where the claimant was not mostly at fault, benefits run up to 104 weeks. Where a damages claim is pending, benefits can last 156 weeks if permanent impairment does not exceed 10%, or 260 weeks if it does. SIRA data to June 30, 2025 show that 97% of claims were accepted for statutory benefits in 2024-25, that about 3,800 claims are reported each quarter, and that 91,313 claims had been recorded under the 2017 scheme since it began, with a further 10,362 expected but not yet reported.

Who is affected

The report identifies three groups. Brokers advising New South Wales clients, particularly fleet and commercial customers whose CTP costs add up across many vehicles, will need to explain renewal pricing. Claimants under the 2017 Act and the two earlier laws receive revised benefit and damages amounts. And motorists generally face Green Slip pricing at renewal.

Wider motor insurance context

The report places the change in a broader setting of rising motor costs, quoting the Insurance Council of Australia, ASIC and others. It says the Council found average motor claim costs rose 42% between 2019 and 2024, and that ASIC reported motor vehicle insurance premiums rose 8% in the 12 months to July 2025. The report adds that those findings relate to comprehensive motor cover and not CTP, and that they indicate the general inflationary environment only.

Limits

This article relies on one trade-press report. The indexation percentage and its effect on premiums are not stated, and the premium data predate the October 2026 change. It is general information, not insurance advice.

key_points: From October 1, 2026, SIRA indexed CTP legal costs, medico-legal fees, weekly payments and non-economic damages under the Motor Accident Injuries Act 2017, and damages under two earlier Acts whose claims remain open.

The adjustment equals the change in NSW average weekly total earnings published by the ABS, and the article does not state the percentage; the new caps are A$3,853 for the weekly statutory benefit and A$521,000 for non-economic loss damages.

The average Green Slip rose A$35, or 7%, in the year to June 2025 to A$536 including levies and GST, still below the pre-reform average of A$935, and the article does not quantify any premium rise from the 2026 indexation.
Total average fund levies rose from A$164.80 to A$190.60 between January 2025 and January 2026, and SIRA's excess-profits mechanism has recovered A$542.9 million from insurers since 2020.
Most injured people can claim statutory benefits for up to 52 weeks regardless of fault, and SIRA data show 97% of claims were accepted for statutory benefits in 2024-25.
why_it_matters: Motorists in New South Wales must buy a Green Slip, and the benefits it funds rise with average earnings each year. Higher caps raise what insurers expect to pay out, which feeds into prices at renewal, so the changes matter to drivers, fleet owners and the brokers advising them.

title: Credit Insurance Protected a Record €9.58 Trillion of Trade in 2025, but Its Share of World Trade Slipped to 14% as Insolvencies Rose for a Fifth Straight Year
summary: The International Credit Insurance and Surety Association reports that world trade protected by credit insurance reached €9.58 trillion in 2025, up from €9.25 trillion, while the share of trade covered fell to about 14% from 15% because trade grew faster than GDP and the euro strengthened, as business insolvencies are forecast to rise again in 2026.
description:
The International Credit Insurance and Surety Association, ICISA, has published figures on how much world trade is protected by credit insurance. Insurance Business UK reported them on October 30, 2026. The details in this article come from that report, which also cites the World Trade Organization, BNP Paribas and Allianz Trade. The original ICISA release and those third-party sources were not reviewed, so the numbers are as reported. The report does not give premium totals, claims paid or recoveries, and this article does not either.

What credit insurance is

When a company sells goods or services on credit, it carries the risk that the buyer will not pay. Trade credit insurance covers that risk: if the buyer becomes insolvent or fails to pay, the insurer compensates the seller. Surety, which ICISA also represents, is different: a surety bond guarantees that a contractor will complete a project or meet an obligation, as in construction, energy and infrastructure. Both products help businesses extend credit with more confidence, and lenders often rely on credit insurance when financing receivables.

The headline figure

According to the report, world trade protected by credit insurance rose to €9.58 trillion in 2025, up from €9.25 trillion the previous year. A simple calculation, made here, shows an increase of about €330 billion, or roughly 3.6%. ICISA members represent about 80% of global premium volumes. They had more than €3.5 trillion of insured exposure related to trade receivables in 2025, plus additional billions in surety bonds. About 70% of the cover in 2025 came from the private insurance market; the report does not describe the remainder.

Why the share of trade fell

Although the amount covered grew, the share of world trade that credit insurance covers fell to about 14% in 2025, from an estimated 15% in 2024. The report gives two reasons. First, world trade grew faster than the economy: it cites the WTO's Global Trade Outlook and Statistics of March 2026, which put 2025 trade growth at about 4.7% against GDP growth of 2.9%. Second, currency movements: the euro appreciated about 17% against the US dollar between January 2025 and January 2026, according to BNP Paribas, and because trade is measured on a dollar-denominated base, this lowers the percentage. ICISA says that in constant dollar terms the coverage share would have risen by four basis points, one basis point being one hundredth of a percentage point. The report cautions that how the metric is built, and currency effects, affect the share, so a falling percentage does not necessarily mean weaker coverage.

Demand and insolvencies

ICISA's third-quarter 2026 Business Sentiment Survey found members reporting continued demand growth for trade credit insurance and surety, with a cautious outlook on claims and insolvencies. The report cites Allianz Trade as saying that global business insolvencies rose 6% in 2025 and are forecast to rise a further 5% in 2026, which would be five consecutive annual increases. ICISA says the insolvency environment is focusing attention on when credit can safely be extended, particularly for companies with high exposure to trade receivables. It identifies geopolitical conflict as among the greatest concerns for the market, with direct and indirect effects on claims and insolvency risk.

How the numbers fit together

Three facts interact. Insolvencies are rising, which raises the chance of claims. Demand for cover is growing, which raises premium volume and insured exposure. And the share of trade covered looks lower mainly because of how trade is measured. A reader could be tempted to say that fewer firms are insured, but ICISA's own constant-dollar calculation points the other way. It is worth noting that this adjustment is ICISA's calculation and the report does not show the working.

What is missing

The report does not give the premium volume, claims paid, loss ratios or recoveries, which are the numbers that show how the insurers are doing. It also does not break coverage down by region or sector, and it says nothing about prices. Those are the measures that matter for judging whether the market is under strain, and readers need ICISA's publications or insurers' results for them.

Why it matters to businesses and insurers

For a company selling on credit, the rise in insolvencies makes the question of how much to extend to each customer more important, and credit insurance is one way to transfer the risk. For insurers, a rising insolvency trend can lead to higher claims, which is why ICISA's members describe their outlook on claims as cautious. For lenders, the amount of trade protected is a sign of how much receivables financing rests on insurance. The report does not predict how claims will develop.

Limits

This article relies on a single trade-press report of ICISA data and cites third-party figures at second hand. Calculations marked as made here are the author's. It is general information, not insurance or investment advice.
source_name: Insurance Business UK, reporting ICISA data (October 30, 2026)
image_alt: Cargo containers at a port representing global trade (illustrative)
key_points: World trade protected by credit insurance reached €9.58 trillion in 2025, up from €9.25 trillion in 2024, according to ICISA data reported on October 30, 2026.

Coverage was about 14% of total world trade, down from an estimated 15%, because world trade grew about 4.7% against GDP growth of 2.9% and the euro rose about 17% against the dollar; ICISA says at constant dollar terms the share would have risen by four basis points.
Allianz Trade reports global business insolvencies rose 6% in 2025 and forecasts a further 5% rise in 2026, which would make five consecutive annual increases.
ICISA members represent about 80% of global premium volumes, had over €3.5 trillion of insured exposure on trade receivables in 2025 and wrote about 70% of cover in the private market.
The report gives no premium totals, claims paid or regional breakdown, and ICISA names geopolitical conflict among the market's greatest concerns.
why_it_matters: Trade credit insurance pays sellers when customers fail to pay, so it underpins much of the world's cross-border trade on credit. Rising insolvencies make the cover more valuable and claims more likely, and the figures show how large that safety net has become.
